8
A ball of mass m is thrown vertically into the air. When the ball has speed v, the air resistance
acting on the ball is F.
What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the ball when its speed is v as it rises and as it falls?

hints: Notice the weight $mg$ always acts downwards, but the air resistance $F$ always opposes the velocity so it changes direction between rising and falling.
Use $F_{net}=ma$ in the downward direction: add forces acting down and subtract forces acting up to find the magnitude of acceleration.
For speed $v$ the drag magnitude is the same $F$, so compare $mg+F$ when rising with $mg-F$ when falling and divide each by $m$.
walkthrough: Draw the forces at speed $v$. Weight is $mg$ downwards in both cases. Drag $F$ opposes motion, so it is downwards when rising and upwards when falling.
Take downwards as positive for the magnitude of downward acceleration. Newton's second law is $F_{net}=ma$.
When rising: $F_{net}=mg+F$, so $ma=mg+F$. Dividing by $m$ gives $a=g+F/m$.
When falling: $F_{net}=mg-F$, so $ma=mg-F$. Dividing by $m$ gives $a=g-F/m$.
Rising therefore has acceleration greater than $g$ and falling has acceleration less than $g$. This is option C.

A.explanation: This subtracts $F/m$ for rising, but drag acts downwards with weight when rising so the net force must be larger than $mg$.

B.explanation: This reverses the effects: rising needs $g+F/m$ and falling needs $g-F/m$ because drag always opposes the velocity.

C.explanation: Rising gives net force $mg+F$ downwards and falling gives $mg-F$ downwards, so $a=g+F/m$ rising and $a=g-F/m$ falling.

D.explanation: This adds $F/m$ for falling, but drag acts upwards to oppose the downward motion so the net downward force must be smaller than $mg$.
